items.title: Intel confirms Nova Lake will use advanced 18A-P node, more details at CES — company says it's taking Panther Lake capacity offline to build more Granite Rapids data center CPUs
items.description: Intel's next-gen Nova Lake desktop processors will be the first client product to use Intel's enhanced 18A-P node, CEO Lip-Bu Tan confirmed in the company's Q3 2026 earnings call.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Intel's next-gen Nova Lake desktop processors will be the first client product to use Intel's enhanced 18A-P node, CEO Lip-Bu Tan confirmed in the company's Q3 2026 earnings call. The chief executive also said that the company intends to share more about Nova Lake at CES in January. The company's chief financial officer shared that Intel intends to take Panther Lake capacity offline to build more Granite Rapids data center CPUs.Go deeper with TH Premium: CPU (Image credit: Tom's Hardware)Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platformsCPU scaling with DLSSIntel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shapeBenchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the priceAMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent "Nova Lake, our first Intel 18A-P client product, is tracking ahead of schedule, with design wins expecting to be twice those of Panther Lake at launch," Tan said in his prepared remarks. "We look forward to sharing more at CES in January."There has been a lot of speculation about what node Intel's Nova Lake CPUs will use, with the rumor mill ping-ponging between Intel 18A and TSMC's N2P. Current speculation says the chip will use 18A-P for the SoC tile while using TSMC's N2P for the compute tile. It seems unlikely that Intel would use its most advanced node for an SoC tile, though it's possible.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Regardless, Nova Lake chips will use 18A-P in some regard. Intel announced in June that 18A-P had entered risk production, and at Hot Chips in August, Intel revealed its next-gen Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids will be the company's first server products to use the enhanced node.Compared to 18A, which is available in Panther Lake and Wildcat Lake products currently, 18A-P comes with a 9% improvement in speed at iso-power, or an 18% reduction in power at iso-speed. Intel has described 18A-P as a drop-in replacement for 18A, allowing designs built for 18A to instead leverage 18A-P without any extra engineering work. You may like Intel's Core Ultra 400 'Nova Lake' launch schedule leaks out Details about Intel's next-gen Nova Lake CPUs keep leaking Intel's next-gen Nova Lake chips may skip bLLC for mobile SKUs and debut on Razor Lake-HX instead, leaker claims For 18A products, Intel says its new Wildcat Lake products that have shown up in devices like the Framework Laptop 12 are increasingly popular. "Demand for our Wildcat Lake is outstripping supply," said Tan. Intel says that 18A products now make up a third of client CPU revenue, up from less than 5% in Q1.It makes sense that those products would be popular given the current environment. Tan said that Intel's OEM partners are "aggressively managing inventory to match softer sell-through," which means buying less to match the demand in the market. Intel's David Zinsner said the company expects the company's client business to decline by "more than 20%" in the next quarter."Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsZinsner warned of a further contraction in the PC market, describing a sustained decline in the size of the market over the next year, at least. "We expect the 2026 PC unit [Total Addressable Market] to decline approximately 12%, with second half units down more than 20%. We do not expect a sustained recovery until memory availability improves and pricing begins to normalize," Zinsner said. "For 2027, we're planning a PC unit TAM to decline roughly 10%."Taking the comments together, Intel is saying that it expects the market itself to shrink significantly over the next year due to memory prices. It's not a situation of demand outstripping supply, at least not directly like the case of a component shortage. Rather, it's a pullback from direct customers, OEMs, and IT departments from spending, which is more significant.Although Intel says the client PC market is shrinking, the company says that its long-term outlook remains positive. "We think next year, and in future years, we're a market-share-gain type of environment... we do think the PC is going to through a renaissance despite [memory shortage]," said Zinsner.Despite the optimism, Zinsner said that Intel is taking some of its client capacity offline to build more data center products. In response to a question about reallocating wafers from client products, here's what the executive said: "Answer: Yes... What we're taking offline to put Intel 3 into Oregon is 18A wafers, which were generally going to build Panther Lake products, so we see the opportunity with some of that capacity freed up to go produce more data center wafers." items.author: Jake Roach
items.titleZh: 英特尔确认 Nova Lake 将采用先进 18A-P 制程，更多细节将在 CES 公布——公司称正将 Panther Lake 产能下线，以生产更多 Granite Rapids 数据中心 CPU
items.descriptionZh:
Intel CEO 陈立武（Lip-Bu Tan）在Q3 2026财报电话会上确认，下一代桌面处理器Nova Lake将成为首款采用增强版Intel 18A-P制程的客户端产品，并称该项目进度领先原计划，发布时客户设计采用数量预计将达到Panther Lake的两倍。公司还计划在次年1月CES上披露Nova Lake更多细节。这使Nova Lake成为观察Intel先进制程落地、客户端CPU路线图以及代工与产品协同能力的关键产品。

背景方面，外界此前对Nova Lake采用何种制程猜测较多，传闻在Intel 18A与台积电N2P之间反复。当前说法是，Nova Lake可能采用混合芯粒方案：SoC芯粒使用Intel 18A-P，计算芯粒使用台积电N2P。文章指出，把Intel最先进节点用于SoC芯粒并不常见，但并非不可能。可以确定的是，Nova Lake会在某些部分使用18A-P。Intel已于6月宣布18A-P进入风险试产，并在8月Hot Chips会议上透露，下一代至强7 Diamond Rapids将是首款采用该增强节点的服务器产品。现有18A已用于Panther Lake和Wildcat Lake等产品。

技术层面，18A-P是18A的增强版本。与18A相比，18A-P在同等功耗下速度提升9%，或在同等速度下功耗降低18%。Intel将其描述为18A的“即插即用”替代方案，原本针对18A的设计无需额外工程工作即可迁移到18A-P。这有助于降低客户迁移成本、提高先进节点量产灵活性，并增强Intel在产品与代工业务之间的协同能力。若Nova Lake确实采用SoC与计算芯粒分用不同节点的方案，也体现出芯粒架构下按功能模块选择制程、平衡性能与成本的思路。

产品和市场进展方面，Intel称18A产品目前已占其客户端CPU收入的三分之一，较Q1不到5%显著提升；Wildcat Lake需求超过供应，并已用于Framework Laptop 12等设备。Nova Lake导入18A-P后，将进一步扩大先进节点在客户端产品中的覆盖，尤其面向桌面高性能市场。陈立武还表示，Nova Lake的客户设计采用数量预计是Panther Lake发布时的两倍，显示Intel对下一代桌面平台的客户导入抱有信心。

不过，Intel同时面临PC市场收缩压力。CFO David Zinsner表示，OEM合作伙伴正积极管理库存，以匹配较疲软的终端销售，预计下季度客户端业务将下降超过20%。他预计2026年PC单位总可服务市场（TAM）将下降约12%，下半年单位下降超过20%；2027年PC单位TAM还将下降约10%。在内存供应改善和价格正常化之前，公司不预期市场持续复苏。文章解释，这并非简单的供不应求，而是直接客户、OEM和IT部门支出回撤，影响更大。尽管如此，Intel长期仍看好份额增长，并认为尽管存在内存短缺，PC仍可能迎来复兴。

产能安排上，尽管长期乐观，Intel正将部分客户端产能转用于数据中心。Zinsner称，公司会把原本一般用于生产Panther Lake的18A晶圆产能释放出来，以生产更多数据中心晶圆和产品，例如Granite Rapids。总体来看，Nova Lake采用18A-P既展示了Intel先进制程的进展，也反映出公司在PC市场疲软和内存短缺周期中，通过混合节点、产能重配和产品节奏维持竞争力的策略。

items.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
items.description: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. items.content: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene (ovstage), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin, developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library, and learn how to contribute. Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab. Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗 Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial. Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics (ovphysx), scene updates (ovstage), rendering (ovrtx) and the user interface (ovui). He also used Astra with SimReady (simready-foundation) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example, then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗 Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗 Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. With Astra, Jebens explored computer-aided design and tooling revisions for robots informed by simulation. The agent measured the available space and designed a wrench the robot could use to reach the suspension’s bolts. Jebens reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. This connects design and tooling decisions to disassembly results, offering a starting point for robot policy training. Explore the Onshape importer guide. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗 Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering (ovrtx), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill. Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗 A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

items.titleZh: 走进 Omniverse：开发者如何借助前沿 AI 智能体将创意转化为仿真
items.descriptionZh:
NVIDIA 正在推动一种新的仿真应用开发范式：把前沿 AI 模型与 NVIDIA Omniverse 库结合，让开发者通过自然语言指挥 AI 智能体完成资产生成、物理与渲染连接、场景校验和应用搭建。Omniverse 库提供 GPU 加速的物理、渲染和传感器仿真能力，OpenUSD 则作为统一的数据与场景描述层。文中展示的智能体包括 GPT-6 Astra，以及传感器数字孪生案例中使用的 Claude Fable 5 智能体。开发者不再需要手工串联全部工具链，而是向智能体描述目标、审查结果并引导修改；智能体可调用 ovrtx 渲染、ovstage 场景更新、ovstream 浏览器串流、ovphysx 物理、ovui 界面，以及 Isaac Sim、Isaac Lab、Newton、Warp 等工具，生成应用代码并迭代验证。这一模式的核心创新在于：把仿真应用开发从分散的工程集成，转变为“自然语言指令+智能体编排+可视化/指标反馈”的闭环，降低物理 AI 仿真环境的搭建门槛。

在具体项目中，NVIDIA 团队展示了多类场景。仓库建筑重建方面，开发者将全景照片与点云测量结合，生成不带内部货架和机械的可编辑、可仿真建筑模型，便于在物理改造前评估仓库布局和自动化方案。燃气轮机数字孪生方面，应用允许用户调整负载、环境温度和燃料成分，比较功率、效率、燃料消耗和设备响应；六个测试流程覆盖负载变化、燃料阀卡滞和排气传感器错误，使用 Cantera 进行热化学计算、SciPy 描述设备动态，并把求解结果映射到 3D 转子动画及温度、压力、流速颜色指示，支持旋转、缩放剖视图以及暂停和拖动仿真响应。

规模化压力测试体现了性能与瓶颈定位能力：在 80 条传送带、40 个机械臂和 800 个箱子的场景中，仿真在 2 分钟测试内以全高清分辨率维持 30 帧/秒，机械臂完成 640 次成功放置。场景首次翻倍时性能低于目标，通过并行执行物理计算、图像渲染和视频准备恢复性能并继续扩展；再次翻倍后性能下降，测试将瓶颈定位到物理与机器人控制流水线，为后续优化提供明确方向。

机器人与自动化案例覆盖柔性线缆布线、CAD 转 SimReady 资产、人形机器人仓库仿真、机器人拆解和“机器人奥运会”。线缆布线使用 Isaac Lab、Newton 物理和 Omniverse 渲染，结合 Robotiq 夹爪与强化学习，将学习的布线动作、位置姿态反馈和纠正调整用于 USB-C 插入；后续将测试摩擦夹持并引入真实机器人可获得的相机和传感器信息。CAD 转 SimReady 案例中，ABB YuMi 机器人从 CAD 文件转换为 OpenUSD，匹配外观并配置关节和碰撞几何，经 SimReady Foundation 要求检查后在 Isaac Sim 中完成四次立方体抓放循环；但估计的物理属性尚未与真实机器人校准。人形机器人案例把 SimReady 仓库和人形机器人变成支持第一/第三人称视角的交互式模拟器，连接 ovphysx、ovstage、ovrtx 和 ovui。拆解案例在 PTC Onshape 中建模汽车悬架并在 Isaac Sim 中配置，智能体测量可用空间并设计扳手，仿真中成功拆除悬架部件。Robo Olympics 使用 Unitree G1 人形机器人测试体育运动动作，Newton 仿真、Warp 加速、ovrtx 渲染，单次跨栏实验在 100 次仿真试验中成功 64 次。

自动驾驶与传感器仿真方面，“Zero to Alpamayo”基于旧金山 Market Street 构建可复用仿真环境，分阶段连接资产创建、交通、Omniverse RTX 传感器仿真和 Alpamayo 驾驶模型，用于比较模型并追踪场景或传感器变化对下游驾驶行为的影响；Cosmos3-Nano 实验则改变录制仿真视频中的天气和光照，比较同一场景下驾驶模型响应。传感器数字孪生案例将 ovrtx 相机和原始 LiDAR 输出与实录数据比较，智能体在约三天内从零创建两个数字孪生并改进两个已有孪生，通过相机和 LiDAR 指标验收，迭代修正缺失对象、几何和材质。

此外，NASA 国际空间站资产被组装为带遥测数据的 OpenUSD 模型，并通过 ovrtx、ovstage、ovstream 在浏览器中呈现，开发者用一次提示完成初始搭建、再用后续提示将场景切换到地球昼侧。房间捕获转测试环境案例则结合 PyCuSFM、FoundationStereo 和 nvblox 将立体相机捕获重建为可编辑 OpenUSD 工作室，使用 USD Content Agents 配置物体运动和交互，并在 Isaac Sim 中修正门、抽屉的碰撞与接触。

SimReady Central Library 在柏林 GTC 发布，提供来自设备制造商和资产提供方的 2000 多个仿真就绪 USD 资产，面向机器人仿真和 AI 工厂数字孪生工作流。一个厨房场景包含 180 个放置对象，来自 63 个独特库资产，并加入 18 个自定义几何体，开发者通过对话引导场景组装并用 Isaac Sim 审查渲染结果。

整体来看，这批项目表明前沿 AI 智能体已能承担仿真工作流中的“编排者”角色：把真实扫描、CAD、传感器数据和 SimReady 资产转换为 OpenUSD 场景，连接物理、渲染、传感器与控制系统，生成可交互应用，并通过性能指标和视觉结果定位问题。其影响在于加速仓库自动化、工业设备运维、机器人学习、电子装配、自动驾驶测试、数字孪生和工程协同等场景的仿真验证；同时，案例也暴露出仿真资产物理属性校准、规模化性能和真实传感器迁移等仍需继续验证的环节。

items.title: Elon Musk's SpaceX buying out 418 homes near flagship AI data center, but only if they drop participation in lawsuit
items.description: The properties will supposedly house SpaceXSI staff while also giving a chance to those who don't want to live near the data center to sell their homes.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 4 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter SpaceXSI, Elon Musk’s data center business powering Grok, is reportedly buying 418 properties in Colonial Hills, Southaven, which sits about half a mile from the powerplant that the company will use to power its data centers in the area. According to The Guardian, real estate agents have been going door to door, offering owners deals on behalf of the company provided that they do not join a class-action lawsuit over the noise pollution coming from the gas turbines that power its GPUs.MZX, the SpaceXSI subsidiary that operates the Colossus II site, circulated an open letter to nearby residents, saying that it “requires property for its business purposes,” with Southaven mayor Darren Musselwhite saying that they will be used to house SpaceXSI staff that the company will need as it expands operations. Musk himself is reportedly staying in the area in an Airstream trailer four nights per week to personally oversee the data center build-out needed to power Grok AI.The bigger issue here, though, is the requirement that sellers must sign an agreement that prevents them from joining the ongoing case against the company for noise pollution. The Colossus 1 and 2 sites have been in hot water since they started operating, primarily for their use of unpermitted turbines and the air pollution that they bring. SpaceXSI has since promised that it will remove all its unpermitted turbines in a year, especially as its 1.2-gigawatt powerplant comes online. However, this apparently hasn’t resolved the noise pollution issue that the community has been complaining about.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: “It sounds like an airplane engine but it’s continuous, it’s incredibly loud. I’ve been woken up at 2am by it, I’ve been woken up at 3am by it. I sometimes have to just get away from it because it makes me so angry,” piano teacher Elizabeth Rose, who lives a couple of miles from the site, told the publication. One of the plaintiffs in the class-action, Jason Haley, also said to The Guardian, “There’s a high-pitched hum and then another sound like an airplane over your house. It’s been so torturous I can’t sleep; I just leave the house or turn on some music until I fall asleep completely exhausted. It drives you insane. You also lose hope because you’re being ignored or dismissed. There’s no escape.”The company has denied all the allegations against it, saying that it has adjusted its power output and installed sound-dampening walls to reduce the impact on the neighborhood. Musselwhite also said that city monitors have not detected the site breaching the local ordinance limit of 70 decibels, although some experts say that persistent noise as low as 50 decibels could have adverse health impacts. You may like SpaceXAI offers 50% Starlink discount to placate data center neighbors; 2,000 have signed up SpaceXAI says it will remove all 69 of its unpermitted turbine power generators, but expects process to take a year Microsoft-backed AI data center faces backlash over alleged unpermitted gas turbines and 1.5M-gallon LNG tank Opposition against the noise pollution and Musk’s purchases aren’t unanimous, though. Some residents aren’t as affected by the noise pollution, while local businesses are experiencing increased activity. Other people have also agreed to sell just so they could get away from the noise. The mayor says that the buyout isn’t intended to turn Colonial Hills into a company town. “The buyout has multiple purposes which are to provide homes for some employees and a goodwill gesture from a good corporate citizen for those who perceive the industrial development near them as negative,” Musselwhite said. items.titleZh: 埃隆·马斯克的SpaceX将收购旗舰AI数据中心附近的418套住宅，但前提是住户退出诉讼。
items.descriptionZh:
埃隆·马斯克旗下为Grok提供算力的数据中心业务SpaceXSI（报道中相关实体亦称SpaceXAI）正陷入一场围绕AI数据中心供电、噪音污染和社区关系的争议。据《卫报》报道，该公司正在美国密西西比州南黑文市Colonial Hills社区购买418处房产，这些房产距离公司用于为该地区数据中心供电的发电厂约半英里。房地产经纪人代表公司挨家挨户向业主报价，但交易条件之一是业主不得加入针对燃气轮机噪音污染的集体诉讼。运营Colossus II数据中心的子公司MZX向附近居民发出公开信，称公司“出于商业目的需要这些房产”；南黑文市长Darren Musselwhite则表示，这些房屋将用于安置公司扩张所需的SpaceXSI员工。报道还称，马斯克本人每周有四晚住在该地区的一辆Airstream拖车中，亲自监督为Grok AI提供算力所需的数据中心扩建。

这一事件的核心争议并不只是土地收购，而是收购附加的“不加入诉讼”要求。Colossus 1和Colossus 2站点自投入运行以来便因使用未获许可的燃气轮机和空气污染问题受到批评。SpaceXSI已承诺将在一年内拆除所有未获许可的涡轮机，尤其是随着其1.2吉瓦发电厂上线。然而，这一承诺显然尚未解决社区居民持续投诉的噪音污染问题。报道中，住在站点数英里外的钢琴教师Elizabeth Rose形容噪音“像飞机发动机，但它是持续不断的，声音大得惊人”，她曾在凌晨2点、3点被吵醒，有时不得不离开家以躲避噪音。集体诉讼原告之一Jason Haley则表示，现场有高频嗡嗡声，还夹杂着像飞机从房顶飞过的声音，“折磨得我无法入睡，只能离开房子或打开音乐，直到精疲力尽才睡着；这让人发疯，也让人失去希望，因为你感到被忽视、被敷衍，无处可逃”。

从技术背景看，生成式AI大模型训练和推理需要大规模GPU集群，数据中心功耗密度和总用电量极高。Colossus II这类AI算力园区需要稳定、快速、可扩展的电力供应。现场部署燃气轮机可以在电网接入受限或扩建周期较长时快速形成自备电源，但燃气轮机同时带来氮氧化物、颗粒物和二氧化碳排放，以及持续机械噪音，通常需要空气排放许可和噪音合规。报道提到的1.2吉瓦电厂规模已相当于大型发电设施，而69台未获许可的涡轮发电机则凸显了快速部署与监管审批之间的张力。公司方面否认相关指控，称已调整功率输出并安装隔音墙以降低对社区的影响。市长Musselwhite也表示，城市监测尚未发现该站点超过当地70分贝的噪音 ordinance 限值；但一些专家指出，即使低至50分贝的持续性噪音也可能对健康产生不利影响。这里形成了关键对比：地方合规以70分贝为阈值，而健康影响讨论关注长期、持续、较低分贝的噪音暴露，监测是否覆盖低频和夜间持续噪音也成为争议点。

收购与诉讼限制条款的影响具有多重性。对SpaceXSI而言，购买周边房产可用于员工住房、形成缓冲区域、减少直接邻里冲突，并在AI算力扩张窗口期保障Grok相关数据中心的建设进度；但要求卖家不加入集体诉讼，可能被视为限制居民通过司法途径寻求救济，带来法律、伦理和公关风险。对社区而言，反对并非完全一致：部分居民受噪音影响较小，本地企业因人口和活动增加而受益，也有人同意卖房只是为了远离噪音。市长称收购并非要把Colonial Hills变成“公司镇”，而是有多重目的：为部分员工提供住房，并作为“好企业公民”对认为附近工业开发负面影响的居民作出的善意姿态。相关报道还显示，SpaceXAI曾向数据中心邻居提供50%的Starlink折扣以安抚社区，已有2000人签约；公司称将移除全部69台未获许可的涡轮发电机，但预计需要一年；微软支持的AI数据中心也因涉嫌未获许可的燃气轮机和150万加仑LNG储罐面临类似反弹。整体来看，这一事件反映了AI算力竞赛下数据中心现场供电模式的监管盲区、噪音与空气污染的社区外部性，以及企业通过房产收购和诉讼限制条款管理扩张风险所引发的治理争议。

items.title: US data centers could wipe out 15 years' worth of progress in greenhouse gas emissions, report claims
items.description: The Sierra Club, one of the oldest environmental preservation organizations in the U.S., has now put forth an estimate that by 2030, U.S. data center buildouts will be outputting as much carbon dioxide as the entirety of Mexico.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 9 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Concerns have been mounting everywhere about the environmental impact of data centers, with alarms ringing at various environmental think tanks. The Sierra Club, one of the oldest environmental preservation organizations in the U.S., has now put forth an estimate that by 2030, U.S. data center buildouts will be outputting as much carbon dioxide as the entirety of Mexico, pushing back progress on greenhouse gas reduction by 15 years, Bloomberg reports. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft)The data center cooling state of playThe custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the priceGTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this yearDemand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsibleThe Club's principal advisor for climate and energy, Jeremy Fusher, puts it plainly: "the numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds." He's referring to an estimate that with the output from pending data center builds, the output from the U.S. power sector is set to put 2.1 billion metric tons of CO2 in the atmosphere by the end of the decade, an uptick of 42% compared to 2025 figures. The researchers' previous estimates were between a quarter and half of the current projections.An increasing number of countries and states are enacting laws demanding that new data center builds have a large portion of their power generated by green sources. However, those laws rarely apply retroactively, and oftentimes have a phase-in period. Even the Irish law on the matter demanding that new data centers be fed by 80% of renewable power only requires that that happens six years after they're powered up.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: In the current AI-driven market, speed of construction is king. Roughly 40% of U.S. data centers are fed by natural gas turbines, and the situation doesn't look like it'll be changing much. It'll likely get worse, as the addition of green sources almost assuredly won't keep up with demand. Much like RAM, GPUs, and storage, turbines were all slurped up by data centers. Their prices have risen by 50%, and production is backlogged for years, with one maker stating it's opening slots for production in 2032.Having said all that, Brendan Pierpont from Energy Innovation, another climate-concerned organization, points out that although the current path looks dangerous for the environment, it's hard to make a hard prediction of how the situation will play out. He justifies his position with common data center roadblocks: the availability of turbines, delays in grid connections, and other delay factors. You may like US AI data centers projected to become the fifth-largest natural gas consumer in the world by 2035 Amazon’s new 7.65GW Texas AI data center power plant could become the largest source of CO₂ pollution in the U.S. Amazon warns $68 billion in blocked data centers threatens US AI lead Truth be told, at this point it's hard to predict how many data centers will actually reach completion, given that requests for permits far exceed available grid capacity across the U.S., and a sizable number of buildouts are encountering strong opposition. Plus, although the AI bubble is still alive and well, concerns started to arise about the economics of hyperscalers, indicating some may go the way of the dodo — and their projects along with them. items.titleZh: 报告称，美国数据中心可能抹去15年来在温室气体排放方面取得的进展
items.descriptionZh:
美国数据中心扩张的碳排放问题正引发越来越多环保智库警惕。彭博社报道称，美国最古老环保组织之一塞拉俱乐部（Sierra Club）最新估计，到2030年，美国数据中心建设产生的二氧化碳排放量将与墨西哥全国相当，并使温室气体减排进展倒退约15年。该组织气候与能源首席顾问杰里米·富舍尔（Jeremy Fusher）表示，相关数字“仍然令人难以置信”。其估算显示，如果待建数据中心项目如期推进，美国电力部门到本十年末将向大气排放21亿公吨二氧化碳，比2025年增加42%；而研究人员此前的估计仅为当前预测的四分之一到一半。

这一问题的核心在于，AI数据中心的高密度计算、冷却和供电需求正在快速推高电力负荷，而当前市场以建设速度为王，绿色电力配套往往跟不上。约40%的美国数据中心由天然气涡轮供电，且这一比例短期内难以明显下降，甚至可能进一步恶化，因为新增绿色电源几乎肯定无法跟上需求增长。天然气涡轮虽然部署相对快，但碳强度高，成为数据中心短期锁定碳排放的重要来源。与此同时，涡轮设备也像内存、GPU和存储一样被数据中心大量抢购，价格已上涨50%，生产排期积压数年，有制造商表示要到2032年才开放新的生产档期。

各国和州层面已开始立法，要求新建数据中心很大比例使用绿色电力，但这类法规通常不具追溯力，且往往设有分阶段实施期。例如爱尔兰要求新建数据中心由80%可再生能源供电，但该要求只在数据中心并网六年后才适用。这种制度设计意味着，在AI驱动的建设热潮中，短期新增负荷仍可能主要依赖化石能源。

不过，Energy Innovation的布伦丹·皮尔庞特（Brendan Pierpont）指出，尽管当前路径看起来对环境危险，但很难对最终结果作出硬性预测，因为涡轮供应、电网接入延迟等因素会拖慢项目进度。事实上，美国各地数据中心许可申请远超可用电网容量，大量建设还遭遇强烈反对；同时，尽管AI泡沫仍在，但超大规模云厂商的经济性已引发担忧，部分项目可能随企业调整而消失。因此，实际有多少数据中心能完工仍存在很大不确定性，但已建和待建项目带来的碳排放压力已成为AI基础设施扩张中不可忽视的约束。

items.title: Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 prices hit $2,000, costing more than the RTX 5090 did at launch and with limited stock available
items.description: It costs just as much to buy an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 right now as the launch price for the RTX 5090, with prices now at least two times higher for this high spec GPU.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 9 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080, Nvidia's second-fastest GPU from its current generation, now costs as much as the RTX 5090 did, on paper, when it launched. Prices have reached $2,000 and higher, with most of the available stock online limited to third-party sellers. If you can find it in stock, it may end up costing you two to three times as much as it did when it launched.The cheapest, in-stock RTX 5080 available to buy from a reputable seller online for delivery is this PNY RTX 5080 for $1,999 from Best Buy, the same price as the RTX 5090's on-paper MSRP. You might otherwise end up paying $2,299.99, at least, for this Asus ROG Astral mode at Newegg, or you could pay nearly $3000 for this Gigabyte RTX 5080 from MemoryC, now priced at $2,983.23.Stock for the RTX 5080 is otherwise limited everywhere, with just one or two available for local pickup (in Best Buy's case), and limited options for delivery. You can also find similar in-store-only pricing at Micro Center, depending on location, which has a Gigabyte card for $1,979.99.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: You'll also see a lot of the listings online from sketchy, third-party sellers.. For instance, you could pay at least $2,211.17 for this PNY RTX 5080 from a third-party Amazon seller. Empowered PC, the seller for this card, has had 81% positive ratings over the last 12 months, with 202 ratings in total.Reputable seller or not, this price scale means you're paying significantly more than the $999 launch price for this GPU. As our GPU price tracking shows, though, this isn't an isolated case. RTX 5080 prices have, like the rest of the RTX 50-series, risen steadily since it launched. However, this is the first time that its price floor has been around the RTX 5090's launch price. That PNY RTX 5080, for instance, was being sold for around $1,500 on average back in August.It's a bitter pill for gamers, though, that the RTX 5080 has now reached and breached the RTX 5090's launch pricing. That GPU has an MSRP of $1,999, although it'll now cost you thousands more. Prices for the RTX 5090 hit as high as $9,500 last month, but the situation is even worse today. What little stock that remains on sale online can be found for as high as $12,000.The RTX 5080 uses Nvidia's GB203 GPU and comes with 10,752 CUDA cores, along with 16GB of GDDR7 VRAM. Unfortunately, it, like the rest of the consumer gaming GPU market, is being affected by AI. Demand for high-end GPUs hasn't stopped, but Nvidia's attention has shifted to the enterprise market. So, too, has the focus of memory manufacturers, meaning DRAM allocations and production lines that would otherwise produce memory chips for graphics cards have instead gone to feeding the demand for high-margin HBM for AI data centers.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsors Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.

items.titleZh: 英伟达 GeForce RTX 5080 价格飙升至 2000 美元，比 RTX 5090 首发时还贵，且库存有限
items.descriptionZh:
Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 是当前世代产品线中速度第二快的消费级 GPU，但据 Tom's Hardware 报道，其市场价格已升至 2000 美元甚至更高，达到 RTX 5090 发布时的纸面建议零售价水平。更严重的是，线上可售库存大多集中在第三方卖家手中，若从非官方渠道购买，实际支付价格可能达到首发价的两到三倍。目前，信誉较好的在线零售商中最便宜且可发货的 RTX 5080 是 Best Buy 销售的 PNY 版本，售价 1999 美元，正好等于 RTX 5090 的纸面 MSRP。其他渠道价格更高：Newegg 上华硕 ROG Astral 型号至少 2299.99 美元，MemoryC 上技嘉 RTX 5080 标价 2983.23 美元。Best Buy 的本地自提库存通常只有一两张，Micro Center 部分门店有 1979.99 美元的技嘉卡。第三方亚马逊卖家的 PNY RTX 5080 最低约 2211.17 美元，该卖家过去 12 个月好评率为 81%，共有 202 条评价。无论卖家是否可靠，这一价格都远高于该卡 999 美元的首发价。

从价格走势看，RTX 5080 并非孤立涨价。GPU 价格追踪显示，RTX 50 系列自发布以来价格持续上涨，但这是 RTX 5080 的价格下限首次接近 RTX 5090 的首发价。例如，同一款 PNY RTX 5080 在 8 月平均售价约为 1500 美元。对游戏玩家而言，RTX 5080 达到并突破 RTX 5090 首发定价令人难以接受。RTX 5090 的 MSRP 为 1999 美元，但如今实际价格已高出数千美元；上月其价格一度高达 9500 美元，目前线上剩余少量库存甚至标价高达 12000 美元。

技术层面，RTX 5080 采用 Nvidia GB203 GPU，配备 10,752 个 CUDA 核心和 16GB GDDR7 显存。CUDA 核心是 GPU 中负责并行计算的核心单元，广泛用于图形渲染和通用计算；GDDR7 则是新一代显存标准，旨在提供更高显存带宽，支撑高分辨率游戏和内容创作负载。然而，当前涨价的核心原因并非产品本身的技术创新，而是 AI 需求改变了供需结构。高端 GPU 需求并未降温，但 Nvidia 的战略重心已转向企业级市场；同时，内存制造商的 DRAM 产能分配和生产线也在向高利润的 HBM 倾斜。HBM 通过堆叠 DRAM 和宽接口实现高带宽，是 AI 数据中心加速器的关键内存，其利润率远高于显卡所用的 GDDR 显存。结果是原本可用于生产显卡内存芯片的 DRAM 产能被 AI 数据中心需求挤占，进一步加剧了消费级显卡的供应紧张和价格上涨。

这一局面将产生多重影响：RTX 5080 作为面向高端游戏、内容创作和本地 AI 开发等场景的显卡，其性价比明显下降，玩家升级成本和 DIY 装机成本上升；消费级 GPU 市场出现高端产品稀缺化、价格金融化趋势；Nvidia 和内存厂商则优先服务企业 AI 市场。简言之，RTX 5080 价格达到 RTX 5090 首发价，是 AI 数据中心热潮挤压消费级 GPU 与 DRAM 产能的直观体现，而非单纯的需求波动。

items.title: Anthropic is asking Wall Street to believe in AGI
items.description:
Today on Decoder, I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document known as an S-1.
Anthropic just filed its S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq, and it could start trading as soon as next month at a valuation of anywhere between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. That would immediately make it one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
But the price tag really isn’t the whole story here. The S-1 document published earlier this week is hundreds upon hundreds of pages filled with details that finally paint a picture of the economics of a frontier AI lab. As you might imagine, that picture is both really complicated and built on a series of very, very ambitious assumptions about the future and what AI will do to it.
So I wanted to have Joey on the show to help break down what this document tells us, both about Anthropic’s finances and the broader AI economy. Joey and his colleagues at SemiAnalysis actually built a model of Anthropic’s finances from the outside back in July, so he’s been waiting for this filing about as eagerly as anyone, and I was excited to hear his take on what we’ve learned and, importantly, what we still don’t know.
Okay: SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart on the Anthropic S-1 and the costs and risks of building frontier AI. Here we go.


This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Joey Brookhart, you are an analyst at SemiAnalysis. You’re also co-lead on SemiAnalysis’ Tokenomics model, which is going to come up a lot in this episode. Welcome to Decoder.
Yeah, thanks so much, Nilay.
I am very excited to talk to you. We’re talking just a couple days after the big Anthropic S-1 was filed. It’s our first look inside of the finances of one of the leading frontier models. What’s your take? What’s your read into it?
It was an awesome S-1. It’s been a rough three weeks since the investor day. Some people were somewhat disappointed in the September [annualized recurring revenue] numbers, but what we saw here was a company that has efficiently scaled to an amazing level, with a $1 trillion-plus valuation, $70 billion-plus of ARR in a very short amount of time.
In gross margins, compute margins, and free cash flow, everything is what you’d want to see. So I don’t think there was much to nitpick in this filing. It’s the reason you’ve seen a lot of the semiconductor complex, and the neoclouds and compute stocks, really rally again in the last two days.
It’s funny, I don’t think I can nitpick the S-1 itself. I want to get into some of the details because there are a lot of numbers in there that are worth thinking about. I actually just want to start at the really big picture. You run a thing called Tokenomics. I’m going to explain what Tokenomics is to people.
I look at Anthropic and where it could go. I look at Dario Amodei saying that he can see his way to $1 trillion in revenue. Where does that money come from? Because so much of these businesses are about eating every other business and it feels like someone else has to make some money to pay Anthropic to generate these revenues. I haven’t actually seen that laid out very clearly.



Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. 
It’s so interesting. Today, because even the scale we’re at is $120 billion of ARR between the two leading labs, it’s still an extremely narrow market. The top 1 percent of customers are the ones that are spending $50,000 to $100,000 per employee. Your broader Fortune 500 or Global 2000, which typically do a lot of IT spend, isn’t spending much.
A lot of the spending, especially at Anthropic, is coding-specific. It’s almost a single vertical company. We look in the future to 2027, you think to this broader adoption and white collar work. This typical enterprise Q4 budgeting season, we actually haven’t gone through with one of these labs yet in any meaningful way because their ARR did really start to accelerate until the beginning of the year. We think of other cases like cyber, which can be similar to coding, where these are eight-figure-plus contracts with leading enterprises that can scale very quickly due to all the cybersecurity incidents we’re seeing. You get to other verticals like bio.
To get to $1 trillion, we do have to move to some of that white collar work, where it goes from AI augmentation to labor saving or replacement in some areas. You look at things like Microsoft’s buyout offers to employees as an example of this, but there’s no wealth of other verticals that they can get into and really start to move the needle.
This is the single biggest question I have, not just about the S-1, but the entire industry. I would understand that if there are one or two leading labs. There are two big companies that have a technology that can automate a whole bunch of things. We will see how well that automation goes sector by sector, but there are not just two leading labs. There are quite a few of them. There are open weight models.
I’ve heard from a lot of CEOs who are very nervous about giving all their data to an OpenAI or Anthropic and they would like to run some things on-prem. There are law firms running on-prem AI now, which is the funniest turn in maybe all of history.
How do you see that playing out? Because so much of the pressure on this S-1 was the numbers themselves, which I want to talk about, but then there’s the external pressure of, “You’ve got to grow and growth is not as short.” So how do you see all of that playing out?
It’s very interesting because when we look at coding today, for example — and I think we saw this in Q3 with OpenAI kind of catching up — there are areas of coding where there are very low switching costs, and I can just move between that. What we hear from enterprises and maybe, too, on the OpenAI side — obviously I think they somewhat botched the Fable release, and the lack of zero data retention is why we saw some of the slowdown. That’s something they can fix with Fable 5.5 and maybe drive more enterprise adoption there.
That’s a huge thing for enterprises when we talk with them. We definitely see enterprises now, and more so, too, a lot of the AI natives, doing custom training and post-training on open weight models, and then running either their inference off of that or even their products for internal or external use cases.
Obviously, DeepMind at Google and [Meta Superintelligence Labs] are very well-funded labs that have pretty similar training compute capacity, and they’re bringing on a ton of it. Not even to mention SpaceX as well, with what Elon said on [about] 10 net new gigawatts next year and half of that is the long-term internal use case.
In the first half of the year, Anthropic ran away with it. They were 90 percent of the industry’s net new ARR. We saw in Q3 that OpenAI was probably actually the majority of industry net new ARR. Open-source has grown from probably $1 billion of token inference costs, ARR, in Q1 to $10 billion-plus here in Q3.
So yes, the industry’s gotten much more competitive, but there are all these new use cases, too, and some of these verticalized use cases are really where we’re going to see the growth going forward. Because it’s obvious coding isn’t going to power us to even triple from here.
It’s interesting. The concept is called Tokenomics. You run that practice alongside another co-lead at SemiAnalysis. Explain what it is because to me it’s such a smart way of thinking about, “We’re going to put some money in and maybe we’ll get some money out.”
I think of it as the unit economics [of AI], or even just the broader idea — everything from a macro- to microeconomics of running an AI business or even looking at AI demand. So we cover the hyperscalers, now some of the neoclouds as well in a separate product.
But then just the AI labs, too. For investors, or just people that are interested in the business, Anthropic had negative 94 percent gross margins on inference two years ago. Now they have a positive 85 percent margin, and people don’t understand how they allocate compute. How do we think about the inference business model?
Part of that gross margin conversation is the revenue per megawatt in inference. Why are all companies that are running inference seeing massive gains in inference and compute efficiency? So we try to model out these businesses and obviously when Anthropic was private, we’re dealing with information we can get from the press and things like that.
But now that we have concrete audited numbers, it’s easy to explain the unit economics of this. And also how the businesses differ. OpenAI is a much different business than Anthropic just in both their consumption versus subscription and then historical weight versus consumer versus enterprise. [We are] trying to understand across the demand level the economics of these businesses.
Several years ago when I talked to Google CEO Sundar Pichai about the cost of inference, I said, “How are you ever going to make money?” He was just very clear. He said, “If there’s one thing Google’s good at, it’s bringing this stuff down the cost curve.”
It was a very blunt answer. I understand how Google can do it. They make their own chips. Anthropic is running on everyone else’s clouds. The core part of the S-1 is how much they’ve committed to spend on other people’s clouds: SpaceXAI, Google, Amazon. Where does their efficiency come from?
There’s really token throughput. They have a very diverse chip fleet. Between Trainiums, TPUs, and GPUs, across all of those, we see a ton of token efficiencies. Token throughput, for example, on Trainium chips is up 5x to 10x year-over-year right now.
Dealing with both the hardware level efficiencies and the software — and how the model interacts with the hardware — there are a lot of token throughput gains where if you’re doing X tokens per second, now you’re doing five or 10 times that just a year later. What they’ll tell you is they see continued compute efficiencies as well going forward.
Max Kan, who co-leads Tokenomics model with me at SemiAnalysis, and I have even published some research on this. Right now, if Anthropic’s at $65 million of revenue per inference megawatt, this was mid-teens last year at this time. What we’ve said on maybe Opus 5.5 on a [Nvidia] Blackwell, you can get to $100 to $120 million of revenue per megawatt.
The big thing here is they’re paying on average now just a little over $10 million per megawatt in [cost of goods sold], or just in compute costs. What you can do with those margins is then reinvest in training.
People don’t realize this, but only about 30 percent of the compute is actually in inference-serving revenue. The rest is for experimentation and research, training models, and post-training models. So there’s a lot of compute that is building the next model and that’s more of the R&D side and where you actually get your returns and defensibility in this business.
Actually, what I was expecting to see in the S-1 was that dynamic play out much more strongly — that Anthropic makes a bunch of money selling the models they have now and there are more customers in the future for the models they have now. That’s going to throw off a whole bunch of margin. And then, because it is Anthropic and they think they’re building a digital god, they’re going to train the next models as much as they can.
That is a very particular Anthropic story. The company is chasing AGI. The people who work there will happily tell you that in the S-1 that Claude might be conscious and this could all go to hell. Anthropic is a very unique company in its conception of itself. But you don’t really see that dynamic playing out in the S-1. They’re managing their training costs against their inference margin pretty well. Do you see that going up or changing in any way?
I agree. Long term, and we’ve even said this internally, they want to actually increase the percentage of training. If you believe you’re building a digital god or going towards AGI, and as long as you have the gross margins of 85 percent-plus on inference to do so, you can.
They’ve grown a lot faster than they thought, and they didn’t expect to be at 11 percent non-gap EBITA margins. They’d love to be closer to zero, or even below that if they could get that compute and allocate it towards training and continue to see these compute efficiencies.
They’ve messaged that, too, to investors in the roadshow. You can look at this S-1 and just the curve of profitability over the last few years and how little cash they burned to get to this point and you can say, “This is a good business model, but we’re going towards AGI. Don’t expect the margin leverage we’re seeing to continue to this level, even though long-term margins can be quite a bit higher.”
There are some real shades of Amazon there. Jeff Bezos famously told investors he wasn’t going to make money until he could make a lot of money. Obviously, Amazon and Anthropic have a lot of back and forth. Maybe there’s some family resemblance there.
But I’m curious, there’s a point of model capability that would allow you to go into more verticals than just coding, right? We might be at it now. The idea of capability overhang exists, the idea that the models we have today could go and take over bio research. They’re taking over mathematics today. There’s a point at which the smartest business decision is to stop training and to just sell your profitable model into more and more companies. Anthropic as a public company will face that pressure.
Do you think they’re organized or structured to fend it off?
Yeah, I think they’re structured well. With some of the voting stock in areas like that, they definitely are. We’ve seen this in tech before and even publicly when Mark Zuckerberg has made these decisions before to invest heavily.
It didn’t always pay off. I just want to point out, it didn’t always pay off.
Yeah, it did not always pay off.
Although you and I technically are in the metaverse right now, by some definition.
[Laughs] Right. But I think that’s something, and there’s an interesting number in the S-1 that 80 percent of revenue in the last three months comes from models released in the last six months.
So then you say, “Okay, 20 percent of the models are like Opus 4.5 in earlier versions.” One thing going forward is that if you’re a frontier model company, you always need to be at the frontier and it’s incredibly competitive.
Wait, can I ask a really dumb question about that?
Yeah.
Why? I think the heart of my curiosity about the industry right now is if you enabled some bleeding-edge technology that could revolutionize the entire world, at some point, the most profitable thing to do is to just go play it out in all the different verticals, right? It’s not to go make the next one. It’s actually to run an efficient model in legal services and medicine and wherever else that there hasn’t been diffusion of AI yet.
This idea that you always have to be at the frontier, that Anthropic always has to be competing with Google and OpenAI and whoever else, I get it from their self-conception. But from a business point of view, an AI-enabled business is going to throw out more money and spend more money with me, the AI provider, and that isn’t necessarily related to being at the frontier.
There are a few portions of that. For new verticals, and this is very cyber specific, if an adversary is using a frontier model, you need to be defending with a frontier model.
Fair enough.
When we talk to some enterprises, it’s not like an email summary where I can run that on open source or Sonnet. There are just certain verticals where having… [For example,] if you were in a legal case as a defendant, would you be okay if your lawyer was using a non-frontier model if the prosecution—
[Laughs] I got bad news for you about what’s going on in the legal market right now.
The competitive dynamics do dictate that. I think from a go-forward perspective, we’ve seen this with open source too catching up in one point, but the demand will be there. [SemiAnalysis CEO] Dylan [Patel] says this a lot. The demand will always be there for frontier intelligence, especially in competitive industries. And there are certain tasks, as you go towards more labor replacement versus labor augmentation, where that also is the case.
At the same time, they are getting more vertical. If you go look at job postings or what they’re hiring for, they’re putting out more of these SKUs and areas, and there’s a lot of beta testing going on like Claude for financial services, Claude for legal, their cyber program. They’re giving away 25,000 of credits per month for people in their cyber program.
That’ll be a huge SKU for them in 2027. Those verticalized areas and then ones that are specifically where you need to be… It’s more adversarial, I should say, or competitive, are the main reasons why. But we can both agree there are areas like email summary and work that definitely doesn’t need to happen [at the frontier].
I’ll just make a dumb comparison to the iPhone. It’s iPhone season. I just reviewed the iPhone Duo. Apple kept the iPhone looking the same for several years now. They build all of the tooling for the new iPhone and then they just reuse it for two or three or four models to get all the value out of that investment back before they move on to the next thing. Apple puts out a new iPhone, and it keeps selling the old iPhone for a while to get more value out of that investment and that development program.
The AI industry does not seem to be doing that. All of their emphasis is on developing the next new thing, deprecating the old thing pretty fast, and moving you onto the new expensive product, while at the same time they’re building the next new expensive product.
At some point it feels like that will rationalize, that there will be something that is worth just collecting margin from while they go invest in the new thing. I just can’t figure out where Anthropic sits in that cycle.
I mean, we do see this. Open source token volumes are picking up and there’s a lot of areas, yes, where the open source models have become good enough. I think on a go-forward basis, you’re like, “Okay, was that because of distillation?” And then the frontier labs have some defensibility actually going forward. I think when we talk to clients, it’s also about how we actually think about frontier versus open source. So something like a Sonnet type model, if you want to do the iPhone 18 versus the SE type analogy.
We do see that dynamic, and obviously with open source, it’s a question of how much that can take. Two, because we’re so early in these verticals, we don’t know what’s going to be fully agentic. There’s no human in the loop where the harness actually has, I should say, some value and defensibility to it.
The big area I’d look at here, especially when we talk to enterprises today, is only the coders are allowed to use the frontier models at a lot of these enterprises. If you’re a non-coder, some of these companies just limit you to Sonnet, if you’re an Anthropic customer. That’s reflective of how management views and wants to budget for this, what frontier intelligence is actually worth to them in certain areas.
In my financial analyst brain, Claude could not build a good financial model six months ago. It’s getting better if you connect it to the right areas, but we’ve gone from something like, “I needed a junior analyst six months ago,” to, “Maybe I don’t as much anymore,” and then, “Will I have a full junior analyst at my disposal anytime or multiple pretty quickly, if I have unlimited token budget?” We just look at that across every vertical and major job category.
The time horizon in each of those categories is going to be different. That’s just one of the bigger questions I have: How quickly do they get to where they think they can go?
I want to dig in on some of the numbers here. The one that jumped out in all of the comment sections on all of the forums and all of our articles yesterday was $80 billion. Anthropic lost $80 billion [in the first half of 2026]. That is related to a technical charge. Can you just explain the $80 billion? Because it doesn’t seem particularly relevant to the revenue and profits they’re talking about.
Yeah, it’s a non-cash charge because their valuation has gone up so much and they’ve issued warrants or convertible notes. You have to account for that in your balance sheet. It’s just a non-cash charge because their valuation has gone up so much since they issued these warrants and notes.
That’s something you would always back out. You can argue on stuff like stock-based compensation. Should we really be thinking about that on a non-GAAP cash basis? Because it’s non-cash, if I just hand employees shares, I have to account for that on my income statement, but I’m not actually handing them pure cash out of my bank balance. So it’s not an area like that. It gets the accounting, the high level. If you don’t know accounting, it looks bad, but it’s because they’ve grown so much and their valuation has gone up so much.
Some of the argument here about that charge is that Amazon was the other party there. Obviously Amazon’s very happy because Anthropic is buying a ton of AWS and sure they’re happy the valuation has gone up, but over time Amazon’s going to get diluted this way. That’s part of the dynamic there.
Anthropic is going to obviously IPO. They’re going to put a bunch of shares in the market. It’s very clear that over time they will issue more shares to raise more money. It doesn’t seem like they’re going to stop wanting to raise money anytime soon.
How are you thinking about that in terms of just investment into a company like Anthropic, that your valuation might be going up, but your actual ownership stake might be getting diluted over time?
The deals have always been very creatively structured.  The number is they’ve actually only burned $10 billion of cash. They have $120 billion-plus of cash and marketable securities in the balance sheet today, and post-IPO, probably another $100 billion.
It’s a great deal for both parties. They only really rent compute. It’s not like they have these massive capital outlays or even rent-to-own. You can make some arguments about certain accounting and there are these massive compute commitment obligations and that’s technically future debt, or that is sitting somewhat off balance sheet essentially. But from a dilution perspective, all tech companies dilute. Are they going to need to raise another $100 billion of debt or equity at some point? Possibly. Can they continue to creatively structure and finance future compute buildouts? Probably as well.
I know there’s been a lot of angst about the future of compute financing and data center financing in the last few weeks. But if you’re Anthropic, if you’re a major lab, a hyperscaler or Broadcom or Nvidia that are backstopping a lot of these deals, that’s probably not going to change anytime soon. So I’m not particularly worried.
As an equity investor, would I be worried about getting super diluted? I don’t think so. If you believe in this long-term AGI bull case and that Anthropic is going to be a leader in this, that probably shouldn’t worry you. You’re probably looking at a $10 trillion-plus business. They can outrun dilution at that point.
Let’s talk about the compute commitments. I saw at least one analysis saying over the next 10 years, it’s $800 billion-plus in commitments to the various hyperscalers and neoclouds. That’s a lot. You’re saying that they don’t have that much money. They haven’t even spent that much money yet. Do you see them generating the revenues to pay off those commitments?
Yeah. I think when people look at the headline commitments, the $500 to $600 billion number over 7 to 10 years, let’s call it, what they’re paying for compute today actually isn’t that many gigawatts. If you think about their spending right now, on average they’re close to $11 million per megawatt in spend, or $11 billion per gigawatt.
If you take that back to the annual level and say, “Okay, the $520 billion number is over 70 years, for example, that’s really not that many gigawatts and they’re going to be well beyond…” When they get to something like 20 gigawatts, the future compute commitments that they’re running essentially is going to be well into the trillions.
So yes, they are going to have the revenue to do so. It’s more about how much revenue they are going to have relative to how much compute. Two, the compute efficiency equation. If they keep getting a lot more revenue out of every inference megawatt, how much do you really want to invest in training and take margins to zero from a rental perspective? Because you can get to something where even 80 percent to 85 percent of their fleet is just on training and research at these kinds of margins.
The revenue is going to scale pretty well. They’re not in any dire situations there. Unless we realize all this revenue disappears or people churn. It’s not like they have to hit a trillion dollars of revenue extremely, extremely quickly to achieve all this and pay for this.
Unless you’re trying to build digital God and unless it doesn’t diffuse across the economy as fast as everyone wants it to. Those are bets, right?
They’re huge bets. The numbers you look at, if you’re really bullish on this ramp into the digital economy, is Anthropic saying within their Fortune 500 customers, they have 50 percent of the Fortune 500 and that is just 0.1 percent of their total customers’ operating expenses. When you look at that on a per user basis, it’s like $8 a month if you believe OpEx doesn’t include the cost of goods sold. If you believe they include the cost of goods sold, it’s sub-$50 per month.
They said the same thing. Of the top 5 percent of Claude Code users, they’re spending $18,000 a year on average, the top 5 percent of users. Their non-Claude Code users spend under $75 a month, well under $75. There’s this huge opportunity, especially when we talk to enterprises and these traditional buyers of IT software.
Penetration is extremely low in traditional white collar work. That’s the big point, too, that there is a large ramp period here of both seats adoption and usage. You can make arguments of who’s going to win in this, but it’s obvious the frontier labs are going to get some portion of this and it’s going to be pretty material to net new ARR next year.
One of the things that’s really interesting about that is we talk about the frontier labs, we talk about the hyperscalers — Anthropic has a lot of wild risk factors in this S-1, including that Claude might be conscious and kill us all.
But one of the most direct and maybe easiest to understand is that AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud are both suppliers and competitors in some real way, particularly Google. And they say, “These relationships could turn.” They have a big relationship with SpaceXAI. Elon Musk is going to train Grok. They’re going to compete with SpaceXAI at some point. That relationship might become precarious.
As you say, they’re only renting their compute. At some point, the market might force them to own more of their compute because their own competitors don’t want to lease their capacity to the leading company. How do you see that playing out?
We definitely see both OpenAI and Anthropic going more direct and not owning the compute, but more rent-to-own, or going through an SPV as some financial sponsors do and producing the compute more directly versus renting.
There are two points to this. Google, from one perspective, is also selling its external chips to customers and saying, “We don’t care to monetize this within Google Cloud or even allocate the share… If you think we’re very chip-constrained, we don’t even care that these are going to DeepMind or internal GCP compute for us to monetize. We’re just willing to become a chip seller.”
Anthropic loves TPUs and there are 3.5 to 4 gigawatts-plus, and probably more in the pipeline, in terms of orders there of Anthropic buying these chips directly to then rent. So yes, the market is good.
Wait, it’s not buying them directly to rent. So they’re buying them into a neocloud?
Yeah, they buy them through an SPV, or the SPV buys them and then they rent it from the SPV.
Got it. Okay.
Even within Google Cloud or AWS or Foundry, Anthropic is massive — 48 percent of their business comes through the Bedrock Foundry and Vertex where people are paying through their existing cloud relationship to access these models. They’re not even talking to Anthropic. You don’t have to interact with the Anthropic sales force.
You mentioned this earlier. This marketing channel where Anthropic gets a rev share.
Right. If you’re AWS and you’re saying, “I’m running Anthropic compute for, let’s say, $10 million per megawatt, but now I’m getting 16 percent of $65 billion-a-megawatt plus the compute costs as well,” so we’re seeing margins at all the clouds go up right now. Part of it is CPU utilization is going up because of all the coding and then some on the [reinforcement learning] side, but these token-as-a-service businesses as we call them — so AWS Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Google Gemini Agent Enterprise platform, which is formerly Vertex — are actually massively increasing the margins on AI at these clouds.
They’re benefiting as well when shareholders are giving them credit for this recently. In Q2, both Azure and AWS had extremely, extremely strong quarters, AWS specifically, on the back of Anthropic’s growth on Bedrock.
Do you think that will keep Amazon from ever wanting to train its own frontier models? They’re doing a good job of letting AWS be the infrastructure for everybody else, but they’re one of the only big tech companies that hasn’t felt the insecurity of not having their own models.
Yeah, it’s interesting. Amazon is very happy to serve a wide variety of customers and they have very little [frontier capability]. When we look at our estimates of training compute, they have the least of any hyperscaler, except maybe Oracle. It doesn’t seem like there’s much strategy there.
I know Microsoft in the last two quarters has been talking about it a little more. AWS on the call has been talking about it a little more, but it’s not huge. They’re not doing it to the same extent that Meta is or trying to be competitive here or even Google with Gemini. Especially someone like Dylan will tell you, if you’re not trying to compete at the frontier, there’s really not a place for you, especially if you’re only dedicating a few hundred megawatts internally. One, internal use case is like serving Amazon retail, but then two, training. There are a lot of commitments to make to be good at this.
It’s a conversation for a different day, but I look at these Microsoft job cuts and I see it as the glimmer of evidence that they’re going to try to compete in the future. They obviously got burned pretty badly by OpenAI.
Yeah. They have, in the new agreement that they signed, the right to monetize OpenAI models for essentially not paying OpenAI anything within that agreement. They’re going to have some interesting things ahead where they monetize the OpenAI models or even through Microsoft 365 Cowork and Copilot applications where they’re not paying OpenAI anything for a frontier model.
The other dynamic here, and you brought it up earlier, is over the last few weeks, there’s just been a lot of stress about neoclouds — whether they will succeed, whether they will fail. I think Elon Musk said there will be a guppy-like extinction event, which is just a brutal metaphor to use to describe a bunch of data centers.
But this is a bunch of circular financing and Nvidia stood a bunch of them up and maybe the hyperscalers are just going to run away with it. Maybe Anthropic’s demand, because maybe they will want to own more of their own compute because renting it is precarious in all these ways.
What do you make of the neoclouds? Do you think they’re going to survive the market actually shaking itself out as these companies go public?
Elon obviously has some incentive to say neoclouds are going to be extinct. ClusterMAX said something else and just does amazing ratings of the neoclouds. There are a lot of neoclouds that are ex-crypto miners that are not good businesses and are not good at operating clusters.
I just want to point out CoreWeave is an ex-crypto mining company, right?
Yeah. I don’t mean CoreWeave, but there are others further down the list. CoreWeave, Nebius, and anyone that has backing or backstops from one of the major labs, hyperscalers, Nvidia, or Broadcom is going to be okay.
It’s that longer tail. Hyperscalers have been 65 percent of CapEx and net new compute brought online. There’s 35 percent of the market that doesn’t have the balance sheets that the hyperscalers have. Both Google and Meta have recently raised or announced they’re going to raise. When we look at the big four hyperscalers, they don’t actually need to raise that money over the next two years, even though CapEx is growing from $1.2 to $2 trillion pretty quickly.
But for a lot of these other neoclouds, if you don’t have that sort of backing, I think it is very hard, even right now, and becoming extremely difficult if you don’t have the backing or backstops from those players to keep building compute. It’s a very, very tough financing market.
One of the things I think is really interesting about Elon in particular talking about neoclouds dying and obviously hyping up his own data center business is he’s trying to put them in space and to get away from the backlash in the United States around data centers in particular.
We have a lot of coverage about data center backlash in the United States, it is slowing down a lot of projects. But at the rate we’re going, if you think the neoclouds are shaky, you might actually end up abandoning a bunch of GPUs and half-built data centers or have them tied up in financing agreements where they can’t be lit up.
What do you make of that? Do you think we actually just need to go to space? Or do you think the market is going to rationalize and actually take advantage of all the compute that is currently allocated but not being used?
We’ll rationalize more so. The market is very good at finding places to put chips here on the ground. Politically, we’ll see what happens next week with midterms and the fallout from that. Obviously, there are some very large sites that still have massive permitting problems. There’s the entire power equation as we look towards next year.
The data centers will be built. There will be a method to get these built. The biggest thing — and the hyperscale CFOs have said this — from an overbuilt perspective and on a relative basis, it’s pretty cheap to build the data center shell. What they can do if they overbuild is they’re going to say, “We’re just not going to take delivery of the chip. We’re not going to buy chips. We’re not going to fill them up.” They’ll just sit empty and chipless. But the majority of the spend is on the chip side.
So if we do end up in a place where we’re actually oversupplied from a data center perspective, I know that’s a little bit different. It’s the exact opposite of what the question was. They have said that from an ROI perspective. This comes back to that larger question of whether we are still going to be super supply constrained. A lot of people now, especially in the last three weeks, are talking about, “Are we in this massive glut of compute as we look towards 2028 actually?”
Because the same thing we talked about from Anthropic going from negative 94 percent margins to positive 85 percent and compute efficiencies mean as you bring on more inference megawatts that are making a lot more revenue per megawatt, all else SQL, you need less compute. So it’s a question of whether we we going to have enough revenue in 2028 to justify the ROI on $2 trillion plus of CapEx.
This is why I spent so much time asking about capability overhang and how good the models are today, because you can see some competitor that is less idealistic about AGI saying, “Actually, we’re going to do a bunch of forward-deployed engineers in all of these verticals where they haven’t taken advantage of AI and sell them high-margin inference because we’ll automate big chunks of their business and they’ll see the return.” Right now, a bunch of the Fortune 500 has not seen a return on AI spending.
So if you’re actually just better at customer service and deployment and productizing the model, you might get way ahead of where Anthropic needs to be because they’re still thinking about AGI every single minute of every single day. I look at Dario standing next to Marc Benioff at Dreamforce and that dude does not want to be there right now. He wants to be thinking about the machine god.
There’s something there where you can just see competitors coming up with an open source model and saying, “We’re actually going to productize this and we will actually take the revenue that everyone else is depending on.”
Yeah, it’s extremely, extremely interesting. In the interim, that’s why it is getting more verticalized because you need something to bridge AGI where it just fully does the job, you need something to bridge the actual model today.
[Laughs] Yeah. We’ll just take that for granted.
To get there, you need some bridges of where it sits with the actual end user at some point. Everything is going to come down to this: Is there going to be some timing or adoption mismatch where we just don’t get the revenue at a certain point of time to justify that chase of “train and compute towards AGI”? That’s a risk.
The other risk we look at is whether we get more models at the frontier even at the open source that are as competitive in coding, where token pricing across the frontier needs to be taken down, because like I mentioned earlier, there are lower switching costs. Even at SemiAnalysis, we went from 95 percent or 90 percent-plus of our usage at the end of Q2 was on Anthropic’s models down to 70 percent after the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT 5.6 and Astra. And then with Opus 5.5, it’s gone back to 90 percent-plus roughly.
It does come back. Even the base of revenue today — and they’ve said that we have net revenue retention of 900 percent, so they’re seeing this massive, massive growth. This isn’t a traditional software business like ServiceNow or Workday, where you have just an incredible logo or gross retention of 95 percent to 98 percent and customers sign these nice three-year contracts, they never churn, they add some seats, and maybe they adopt another product that is being upsold. This is purely consumption.
The other portion was the 20 percent drop in the last two weeks of the year versus the prior two weeks last year in token spend, because of the holiday season. You’re not going to do work code stuff, you’re not going to be coding for work during the holidays. This is extremely, extremely pure consumption business, even different from how we think about Snowflake or Datadog today in public markets.
Obviously, Anthropic is not the only company that’s going to have an IPO. OpenAI is right next to them. They’ve delayed theirs. You mentioned earlier Anthropic is much more enterprise focused. I think OpenAI for a long time thought that Google wouldn’t react to them and they would just take the search business away and everything would be fine. Google obviously reacted for better or worse. Search is now AI Overviews.
Looking at the Anthropic S-1, what are you looking ahead to with OpenAI? Because they are a more consumer facing company.
